data.title: Does mTORC1-selective dosing extend lifespan, and is rapamycin's glucose intolerance a cost at all?
data.evidence_stands_at: Clinical outcome in humans (oncology); no ageing endpoint
data.gap: The lifespan benefit of rapamycin is strongly linked to mTORC1 inhibition, whereas chronic disruption of mTORC2 is a major mechanism behind the insulin resistance (LAM2012). The separation is well supported but NOT exhaustive: this Atlas's own S6K1-IRS1 edge records that the contribution of the S6K1->IRS-1 feedback arm to rapalog dysglycaemia in humans has never been apportioned against mTORC2 loss, so 'all benefit = mTORC1, all harm = mTORC2' overstates what has been shown. ARR2015, read in the full text, is narrower than it is usually quoted. Daily 2 mg/kg rapamycin impaired glucose tolerance (ARR2015: +71% AUC) and inhibited BOTH mTORC1 and mTORC2 (AKT-S473). Every-5-days dosing left glucose tolerance, fasting glucose and insulin, and beta-cell function intact. But three things were NOT spared, and they matter to this question. Pyruvate tolerance was still significantly impaired, which the authors call surprising and which indicates raised hepatic gluconeogenesis. The impact on T cells was reduced but still significant -- that is the authors' own wording. And mTORC1 inhibition was NOT continuous across the interval: S6 phosphorylation was back to control level by day 5 in muscle, liver, heart and islets, with adipose tissue the single exception, and the paper states outright that the regimen does not continuously inhibit mTORC1 throughout the 5-day period. Intermittent dosing in ARR2015 also still cost roughly 60% of testes mass. So what ARR2015 demonstrates is that the glucose-tolerance harm can be removed by pulsing the drug, not that mTORC1 suppression is maintained while harm falls away. Two further wording points. 'No detectable mTORC2 inhibition under this assay' is not the same claim as 'mTORC2 was not inhibited'. And a pharmacodynamic readout is not a benefit: ARR2015 carried no survival or healthspan endpoint, and its cohort was young male C57BL/6J mice only. For intermittent dosing that does carry a survival endpoint, see ARR2016 (every 5 days from 20 months, female lifespan extended). Dose-response MIL2014 (4.7/14/42 ppm; top dose +23% M / +26% F). PEARL tested 5 vs 10 mg/week but its primary endpoint was visceral fat (missed) - no mTORC1-selective human aging readout exists. Early clinical evidence now exists outside the rapamycin/rapalog class. Bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors (>25-fold selectivity over mTORC2) were validated preclinically (MEN2023: RMC-6272 overcomes drug resistance via complete mTORC1 suppression, sparing mTORC2) and clinically (SCH2025: RMC-5552 Phase 1, n=57 solid tumors) -- treatment-related hyperglycemia was only 4%, which is consistent with the hypothesis that sparing mTORC2 reduces the glucose-intolerance signature seen with chronic rapamycin/rapalogs. Because SCH2025 was open-label, single-arm and had no rapamycin or ATP-site comparator, the low hyperglycaemia rate is a supportive signal, not a causal attribution: it is compared against historical rapalog experience, not against a randomised control. This is the strongest human evidence yet for the mechanistic premise of H2, but it is preliminary, and it comes from an oncology trial, not an aging/longevity endpoint -- the missing link is still a healthspan/lifespan readout for a selective inhibitor.
data.gap_beginner: The lifespan benefit of blocking mTOR is closely tied to mTORC1, while the main side effect (insulin resistance) comes largely from also disrupting mTORC2. That split is well supported, but it is not the whole story - a feedback loop through S6K1 also contributes to the blood-sugar problem, and no study in this Atlas works out how much each one matters in people. In mice, giving rapamycin less often (weekly instead of daily) avoided the glucose problems while keeping the mTORC1 effect, with no mTORC2 effect detectable - which is not quite the same as saying mTORC2 was untouched. Note what that study did and did not measure: it used young MALE mice only, it looked at side effects only, and it never checked whether the animals lived longer. The study that did show a less-frequent schedule still extending life found it in FEMALE mice only. So the two halves of the story come from different sexes, and neither study did both jobs. Newer drugs aimed only at mTORC1 showed a low rate of blood-sugar side effects in an early human cancer trial: encouraging, but that trial had no comparison group and was not about ageing.
data.changed_since_written: 2025: a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor reached humans. In a phase 1 trial of RMC-5552 (Schram, Clin Cancer Res 2025, PMID 41056387, n=57) treatment-related hyperglycaemia occurred in 4% and was not dose-limiting — but mucositis occurred in 49%, so the dose-limiting toxicity moved rather than disappeared. The mechanistic premise also firmed up: bi-sterics reactivate 4E-BP1, which rapalogs cannot, while sparing mTORC2 (Mahauad-Fernandez, Cell Chem Biol 2025, PMID 40803322). A 2026 study extended in vivo bi-steric efficacy from oncology into a cardiac disease model: in mice with pressure-overload cardiac hypertrophy, RMC-6272 showed greater mTORC1 potency and selectivity than rapamycin or Torin1, prevented pathological hypertrophic growth and preserved cardiac function, including when given after hypertrophy was established (Rogge, J Mol Cell Cardiol Plus 2026, PMID 42088305). It is not the first mammalian in vivo efficacy evidence for the class: MEN2023, already in this corpus and cited in this question, reported RMC-6272 tumour regression and growth inhibition in mouse xenograft and patient-derived xenograft models of breast cancer. The 2026 result is organ function in a disease model, with no glucose endpoint. On lifespan: no bi-steric has been tested for lifespan in any mammal, and that is the gap this question turns on. There is one lifespan result for the class in a far simpler organism — rapalink-1, which its authors describe as a bi-steric third-generation TOR inhibitor, prolonged chronological lifespan in fission yeast with a distinct TORC1-selectivity profile (Kumar, Commun Biol 2025, PMID 41023123). A single-celled chronological-ageing assay is not a mammalian lifespan study, so it does not answer this question, but it means the class is no longer entirely untested for lifespan.
data.still_open: Two things this question had merged. First, does a bi-steric extend lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice? Untested, and not in any ITP cohort. Second, is rapamycin's glucose intolerance costing anything at all? Lamming 2012 already reported lifespan extension as separable from glucose homeostasis (in female mTOR/mLST8 double-heterozygous mice), and the highest ITP rapamycin dose produces both the largest lifespan gain and glucose intolerance — so the penalty this question proposes to remove may be a biomarker rather than a cost. A further complication: in male mice, lifespan extension by acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol travels with raised hepatic mTORC2 signalling (Garratt, Aging Cell 2017, PMID 28834262), so mTORC2 tone is not purely a side-effect channel.
data.hypothesis: An intervention that suppresses the mTORC1/4E-BP1 arm while sparing mTORC2 -- now achievable with bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors (RMC-6272/RMC-5552) in addition to intermittent/low-dose rapamycin -- yields the lifespan benefit without glucose intolerance.
data.hypothesis_beginner: Educated guess: a drug (or dosing schedule) that blocks mTORC1 while leaving mTORC2 alone should give the longevity benefit of rapamycin without the blood-sugar downside.
data.how_to_test: Two experiments, not one. (a) Bi-steric (RMC-6272 class) in an ITP-style lifespan protocol at a dose achieving measurable 4E-BP1 dephosphorylation — the actually untested claim. (b) To test whether the metabolic penalty is a cost: normalise glucose tolerance on top of 42 ppm rapamycin, with acarbose or an SGLT2 inhibitor, and ask whether lifespan moves. Note that bi-sterics (deeper, continuous suppression) and intermittent rapamycin (shallower, pulsed) are opposite manipulations and predict opposite things for muscle and immunity; they should not be pooled as one strategy.
revision_log: 2026-08-30: The opening sentence previously read 'Longevity comes from mTORC1 but chronic rapamycin's harm comes from mTORC2 disruption', and the ARR2015 clause read 'inhibited mTORC1 only'. Both were more certain than the experiments support, which is a preferential separation.
2026-09-29: The Lamming 2012 result is now qualified as female mice.

2026-10-03: MARCHANT2026 added - shows in mice that constitutive skeletal-muscle mTORC1 activation raises inflammatory markers but is not sufficient to impair glucose tolerance, weakening the assumed mTORC1-to-glucose-intolerance link at the centre of this question (mouse, muscle-specific genetic model).

2026-10-03: WAN2026 added - shows in Drosophila that lowering the rapamycin-resistant 4E-BP/TOP-translation arm of mTORC1 output extends lifespan without a reproductive cost, supporting the arm-selective premise of this question while saying nothing about mTORC2 sparing or glucose tolerance (fly genetics).
2026-10-03: title rewritten as a question to match Still_Open (was: "mTORC1-selective (mTORC2-sparing) dosing captures longevity without insulin resistance"). URL locked to the old slug via URL_Slug.

2026-10-07: Rogge 2026 (PMID 42088305) added - first in vivo bi-steric efficacy data in a mammal, mouse cardiac pressure overload. Organ function only, no lifespan and no glucose endpoint, so the 'no lifespan data for any bi-steric in any species' sentence stands as written (revision of all 17 cards against the literature).

2026-10-10: Audit N03. Two corrections. The card dated the first mammalian in vivo efficacy evidence for a bi-steric to 2026, but MEN2023 - already in this corpus and cited in this very question - reports RMC-6272 tumour regression and growth inhibition in mouse xenograft and patient-derived xenograft models; checked in the primary full text. The 2026 cardiac study extends that evidence into a new disease model rather than opening the class, so the 2026-10-07 entry above is wrong on that point. Separately, the ARR2015 clause called preserved mTORC1 inhibition a decoupling of benefit from harm, although ARR2015 measured side effects only and ran no survival endpoint; ARR2016 is now named as the intermittent-dosing study that does carry one.

2026-10-10 (re-audit, later the same day): TWO FURTHER CORRECTIONS, both overturning entries above. (1) 'No lifespan data exist for any bi-steric in any species' was false, and the 2026-10-07 entry claiming the sentence 'stands as written' was wrong. Kumar, Commun Biol 2025 (PMID 41023123) reports that rapalink-1, which its own authors call a bi-steric third-generation inhibitor, prolongs chronological lifespan in fission yeast. The claim is now scoped to mammals, with the yeast result named. (2) The ARR2015 passage claimed 'preserved mTORC1 inhibition' and 'continued mTORC1 suppression' and badged itself QUANTIFIED (full text). The full text (PMC4717280) says the opposite on continuity - 'our intermittent rapamycin regimen does not continuously inhibit mTORC1 throughout the 5-day period', with S6 phosphorylation back to control by day 5 in muscle, liver, heart and islets and adipose the lone exception. The paper's Introduction does say inhibition is 'sustained in many tissues', which is where the Atlas wording came from, but that is the framing its own Results and Discussion contradict. The passage now also carries the pyruvate intolerance, the reduced-but-significant immune impact, the ~60% testes-mass loss and the young-male-only cohort, all of which the 'largely spared' reading had dropped. The self-certifying 'QUANTIFIED (full text)' badge is removed: a badge asserting full-text verification on a statement the full text refutes is worse than no badge.
